steps.title: A first orbit
steps.caption: A single-stage rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral at Apollo 11's launch time. It climbs straight up, tilts over, and lets gravity bend its path round (orange: engine burning). When the top of its path reaches 200 km it shuts down, coasts up (blue), and fires again to make the orbit circular. The yellow line is its track over the ground.

steps.title: Why rockets tilt over
steps.caption: Nine launches, each tilting a different amount after liftoff. Tilt too little and the rocket climbs steeply, spending its propellant holding itself up against gravity. Tilt too much and it turns over into the ground. In between, it reaches orbit. The Sweep tab lists every flight; click one to look at it.

steps.title: Pushing through the air
steps.caption: Rockets with blunter and blunter shapes. The air pushes back hardest about a minute after liftoff, around 10 km up, when the rocket is already fast but the air is still thick: that peak is max-Q (the pink graph). A blunt rocket loses hundreds of metres per second to the air, and the bluntest ones never reach orbit. That's why rockets are long and thin.

steps.title: Dropping dead weight
steps.caption: The same rocket cut into two stages. When the first stage's tanks are empty, it is dropped and falls back into the Atlantic (grey), and a smaller engine carries on with a much lighter rocket. Without the empty tanks, the same propellant gives 4 km/s more. Nearly every real rocket has two or three stages.

steps.title: Your own flight program
steps.caption: Every flight is a list of steps: burn or coast, which way to point, and when to stop. This one reaches a low orbit, then raises it to 1000 km with two short burns half an orbit apart, the cheapest way between two circular orbits. The steps are in the Flight program tab under the 3D view: change them, or customize any example's.

steps.title: A knife edge
steps.caption: The same rocket, but burning until its tank is empty, with no second burn, and (to give it a chance) without air. Now orbit is only reached in a thin band of tilt angles, and only just: the turn has to level off at the very moment orbital speed is reached. With air, none of them make it. This is why real rockets coast up and burn again.

steps.title: Latitude sets the tilt of the orbit
steps.caption: Launching due east from different latitudes, seen edge-on from where the orbits cross the equator. Each orbit is tilted (inclined) to the equator by exactly the launch latitude: blue, from the equator, lies flat; red, from 60°, is steepest. Launches nearer the equator also get more help from the Earth's 465 m/s spin, so many spaceports are as close to the equator as their country allows.

steps.title: East versus west
steps.caption: From the equator, launch directions from due east (blue) round to due west (red). Going east, the rocket keeps the ground's eastward speed; going west it first has to cancel it, costing about 930 m/s more. Westward orbits run backwards (retrograde).

steps.title: A polar orbit
steps.caption: Seen from above the north pole: a launch south from California into a polar orbit. The orbit stays fixed in space while the Earth turns beneath it, so each pass crosses the ground further west. Over a day, a polar satellite sees the whole planet.

steps.title: To the Moon
steps.caption: Launched at Apollo 11's time, on the direction that puts the orbit's plane through the Moon: 72.3°, close to Apollo's 72.0°. After a parking orbit, the trans-lunar injection burn stretches the orbit out to the Moon. Three and a half days later the rocket meets it. We're looking down on the plane of the journey.

steps.title: Arriving at the Moon
steps.caption: Close up, centred on the Moon. The rocket swings in, fires its engine against its speed relative to the Moon, and is captured into an orbit about 650 by 10,000 km above the surface: an orbit lasting about 15 hours.

steps.title: Timing is everything
steps.caption: The same trip, starting the injection burn up to a minute earlier or later. Aimed at the centre, the rocket hits the Moon; a few thousand kilometres either side, it brakes into orbit. Ten seconds of timing moves the arrival point by about 2300 km.

steps.title: Launch windows
steps.caption: Launching due east at different times of day. The orbit's plane is fixed when the rocket leaves the pad, and the turning Earth swings that plane round: only around 03:15 UTC does it pass through the Moon. That is a launch window.

steps.title: A gravity assist
steps.caption: Passing close behind the Moon, the rocket is swung round and gains energy from the Moon's motion, enough to leave the Earth for good. Space probes use the same trick on the planets. That's the tour: every scenario is under File ▸ Examples, ready to change.
